message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This review is grounded in two months of actual till data for every main course, a full competitor price check, and the latest supplier information, so the recommendations are not guesswork. The price increases are modest and targeted: each of the three dishes stays below the midpoint of competitor prices for that dish, so we remain the value option in the area, and with 60% of bookings from repeat guests our customer base is loyal enough to absorb a pound or two. The projected effect is simple to check, £810 a week or about £42,000 a year in additional gross profit, which lifts our main-course margin to about 71%. I also think the menu-mix decision is clear-cut: the data show the mushroom risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so replacing it with a seasonal special is an easy improvement. Monitoring for eight weeks gives us an early warning if volumes move. Overall I believe these changes are sensible, low-risk and well evidenced.
</author>

<document>
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.
</document>
response:
## What the author says the review shows

1. It's based on two months of till data, a full competitor price check and current supplier information.
2. The price rises are modest. Each dish stays below the competitor midpoint, so the restaurant remains the value option, and with 60% repeat guests the customer base will absorb the increase.
3. The rises add £810 a week (£42,000 a year) in gross profit and lift the main-course margin to about 71%.
4. The mushroom risotto has the weakest margin and the lowest sales, so replacing it is an easy decision.
5. Eight weeks of monitoring will give early warning if volumes fall.

The arithmetic in Table 1 and the competitor-midpoint check are correct. But the risotto decision rests on a misreading of the table: the risotto has the **highest** margin on the menu, not the weakest. The profit projection also leaves out the 12% beef price rise that takes effect on the same day as the new prices, and it probably counts VAT as profit.

## Checks that pass

- **Table 1 margins:** fish 69%, burger 72%, curry 75%, steak 60%, risotto 80%.
- **Weekly plate count:** the rows add up to 1,050.
- **Competitor midpoints:** fish £17.98, burger £16.50 and steak £29.50. All three new prices sit below these.
- **The £810:** £1 × 310 + £1 × 260 + £2 × 120 = £810 a week, or £42,120 a year.
- **The ~71% margin:** this is about right on the paper's own basis, before the beef increase.

## Major issues

**1. The risotto has the best margin, not the weakest.**

| Dish | Margin | Gross profit per plate |
|---|---|---|
| Mushroom risotto | **80%** (highest) | **£11.20** |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 |

The risotto beats the burger and the curry on cash per plate as well as on percentage. Its sales (90 a week) are also tied with specials for lowest, not uniquely lowest.

A high-margin dish with low sales usually calls for better placement or promotion, not removal. The proposed replacement also falls in a category, specials, that runs at a 64% margin. If the risotto is the main vegetarian option, removing it also risks losing mixed groups that include a vegetarian. As written, this proposal would probably reduce profit.

**2. The 12% beef increase isn't in the projection.**
Section 4 says beef rises 12% from 1 April, the same day as the new prices. The steak's £2 rise and the burger's £1 rise are counted in full, with no allowance for higher beef costs. If the entire food cost per plate were beef, which is an upper bound:
- steak cost goes up by about £1.25 a plate, which on 120 plates is £150 a week;
- burger cost goes up by about £0.50 a plate, which on 260 plates is £131 a week.

That's up to about **£281 a week** of the £810 gone. At the upper bound, the steak margin would fall to about 58%, *below* today's 60%, despite the price rise.

**3. VAT is probably counted as profit.**
UK menu prices include 20% VAT. If that applies here, a £1 rise on the menu brings in about 83p for the restaurant, so £810 becomes about **£675 a week** before the beef increase. It's worth checking how the accounts calculate margin. Whichever basis is used for percentages, the cash figure has to exclude VAT.

**Combined:** realistic additional gross profit is roughly **£400–675 a week (about £20,000–35,000 a year)** if volumes hold, not £42,000. The exact figure depends on the beef share of each plate's cost.

## Other points

- **The restaurant won't remain the cheapest.** Today the restaurant is the cheapest of the group on all three dishes. After the rises, each dish is priced above the lowest competitor (fish £16.95, burger £15.50, steak £27). "Below the midpoint" is accurate; "the value option" is no longer clearly true.
- **Repeat bookings aren't the same as price tolerance.** The 60% figure shows loyalty, not willingness to pay more. Regulars are also the guests most likely to notice the changes, especially since the plan is not to draw attention to them on the menu.
- **There's little room for volume to fall.** Before the beef increase, gross profit drops below today's level if volumes fall by more than about 8% on fish, 8.5% on burgers and 11% on steak. With the beef increase factored in, the margin on burgers and steak is tighter still.
- **The monitoring baseline is seasonal.** January and February are usually quiet. Spring trade may rise anyway and hide any drop caused by the higher prices. Better comparisons would be April–May of last year, or each dish's share of total main courses.
- **"Weekday lunch is a small share" isn't supported.** The paper only says Friday and Saturday dinner is just under half of sales. Nothing shows the lunch share.
- **Trading days are inconsistent.** Section 2 says the restaurant opens Wednesday to Sunday, which is five days. Section 8 says "six trading days a week."

## Settled and open

**Settled by the paper's own figures:**
- The risotto has the highest margin on the menu.
- The projection omits the beef increase.
- The new prices are below the competitor midpoints but no longer the lowest.
- The trading days are stated inconsistently.

**Open, with what would settle each:**

| Question | What would settle it |
|---|---|
| Beef share of the steak and burger costs | Recipe costings |
| Whether the margins and £810 include VAT | How the accounts calculate gross profit |
| Whether volumes hold at the new prices | Weekly monitoring against a seasonally matched baseline |
| Whether the risotto's low sales are about the dish or its position | Moving it on the menu or having staff recommend it for a few weeks |

## Recommendation

The price rises are reasonable and probably still worthwhile. Before approval, the paper should:
1. Restate the projection net of VAT and the beef increase, as a range.
2. Consider a larger steak rise, since beef could otherwise erase most of its gain, and £28 still leaves room below the £29.50 midpoint.
3. **Drop the risotto proposal**, or reverse it: promote the risotto.
4. Fix the monitoring baseline and the trading-days error.
